metas.name: Agriculture - Coffee
metas.note: Coffee beans are by far the most common in Minas Gerais, but also can be found in Espirito Santo and northeastern Sao Paulo.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Agriculture - Cotton
metas.note: 73% of Cotton Production in Brazil takes place in Mato Grosso. 20% take place in the western border of Bahia. Other minor spots are western Minas Gerais, Southern Goias and Northern MGDS
metas.footer: Brought to my attention by [ODG] Felix

metas.name: Agriculture - Eucalyptus Grandis
metas.note: Eucalyptus Grandis, when fully grown, is a very tall tree with plantations all over Brazil. You can find them in both large and very small plantations, as well as randomly growing anywhere. You can see them all over the south, but there are some large plantations in Amapa too.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Agriculture - Soybeans
metas.note: Soybeans appear as small, leafy soil grown plants. They are most commonly grown in Mato Grosso, Paraná, and Goiás.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Agriculture - Sugarcane
metas.note: Sugarcane plantations are by far most common in the state of Sao Paulo, and in the coastal north east states, especially Alagoas and Pernambuco.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Architecture - European Architecture
metas.note: Buildings in the southern states, mainly Santa Catarina, can be of European influence (typically vaguely German) in design and style.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Architecture - Red Brick Architecture
metas.note: Houses made out of red brick are more common in Northeastern Brazil.
metas.footer: Source: self-researched

metas.name: Architecture - Stilt Houses
metas.note: Wooden houses on stilts are very common in the state of Acre.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Car Meta - Noronha Car Meta
metas.note: Ilha de Fernando de Noronha is covered by a white buggy which sometimes has a visible front.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Coverage Meta - Amapa Blur
metas.note: In all Generation 4 coverage in Amapá, the front right of the camera is smudged. In addition, all Generation 4 coverage in Amapá features the white car with the blue stripe.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Coverage Meta - BR-156 in Northern Amapa
metas.note: This road is characterized by the Amapa Blur (slight blur at the front of a blue-striped car), the red, and the road angle to Northwest. There are frequently Areca palms growing near this road.
metas.footer: Source: Unique Roads of the World by Figsy

metas.name: Coverage Meta - Camera Glitch
metas.note: Northwest Rio Grande do Sul has coverage with this camera glitch in Generation 3.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Coverage Meta - East-West BR156 in Amapa
metas.note: This part of the BR156 can be recognized by the Amapa Blur (slight blur at the front right of the blue-striped car). It's the only Amapa Blur coverage on a road that goes East-West. This part of the road is paved.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/brazil for more clues.

metas.name: Coverage Meta - Extreme Blur
metas.note: White car with blue stripe in combination with an extreme blur on the front right is common in and around Porto Alegre, RS.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: Coverage Meta - Flooded Coverage
metas.note: Flooded coverage can be found between Macau and Macauzinho in Rio Grande do Norte.
metas.footer: Source: Unique Roads of the World by Figsy

metas.name: Coverage Meta - Hazy Sky
metas.note: Hazy Sky Coverage is very common in Porto Velho.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Coverage Meta - Post Bushfire Coverage
metas.note: The road between Caico, RGDN and Santa Luzia, Paraiba is unique with its post bushfire coverage. The part in Paraiba often has outer dashed lines
metas.footer: Source: self-researched by me and Figsy

metas.name: Coverage Meta - Rifts
metas.note: You can often see rifts in Alagoas Generation 3 coverage.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Coverage Meta - Smoke Coverage
metas.note: Smoke Coverage in Brazil can be found along the TO-335.
metas.footer: Source: Unique Roads of the World by Figsy

metas.name: Infrastructure - 2 Ridge Insulator
metas.note: Memorize the distribution map.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Insulators by samuel8170

metas.name: Infrastructure - 3 Ridge Insulator
metas.note:
Most commonly found in Paraiba in the North, and in Parana, Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro. It's pretty rare.

Memorize the distribution map for more details.

Note by MB: They're also different to the lollipop insulator, where the ridges have different sizes.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Insulators by samuel8170

metas.name: Infrastructure - 4 Ridge Insulator
metas.note:
Widespread, but can still resolve some 50/50s. Memorize the map.

Also, in Sao Paulo, it's common in Sao Paulo city, and uncommon outside of it.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Insulators by samuel8170

metas.name: Infrastructure - 5 Ridges Insulator
metas.note: Insulators with 5 ridges are very common in Sao Paulo.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Insulators by samuel8170

metas.name: Infrastructure - 90° Crossbar
metas.note: Right angle top bars are common in Brasília
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Aerodynamic Lamp
metas.note: Aerodynamic Lamp Heads are common in Fortaleza.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Alagoas Lamp
metas.note: Different colors possible
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Aracaju Lamp Arm ID
metas.note: Unique ID on a common lamp head. Sometimes, you can't see much of the code, only zip ties.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Aracaju Road Sign
metas.note: Aracaju, Sergipe
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Barra Do Garcas Lamp Arm
metas.note: Barra Do Garcas, Mato Grosso (border to Goias)
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Belem ID
metas.note: Lots of rare pole IDs in the city
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Belo Horizonte Lamp
metas.note: Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Bend Attached to Pole
metas.note: The vast majority of poles in Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Pará, Amapá, Rio Grande do Norte, Pernambuco and Santa Catarina have the lamp arm attached to the pole, as opposed to it being attached with a plate, which is much more common generally.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Big Electricity Counter on Pole
metas.note:
Big electricity counters on the pole are most common in Mato Grosso, Para and Amapa.

Unlike their smaller version, they do not appear in Paraiba.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Black&Yellow Bollards
metas.note: Black & Yellow bollards of different kinds are common in Salvador.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Blue ID
metas.note: Unique to Rio Branco
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Blue Lamp Arm ID
metas.note: Small, blue, hanging from the lamp arm. Found in Cuiaba (bend attached to pole), and in the cities of Riberao Preto and Sao Paulo (normal lamp arm)
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Boa Vista ID
metas.note: Boa Vista, Roraima
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - BR-101 in the Northeast
metas.note:
This road is divided. What makes it special is that one direction as asphalt and the other direction has concrete pavement.

This does not apply to the entire road anymore
metas.footer: Source: Unique Roads of the World by Figsy.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Brasilia Streetsign
metas.note: Brasilia, Distrito Federal
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Brown Mushroom Insulator
metas.note: Pernambuco sometimes uses these brown mushroom insulators.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Campinas Sidewalk
metas.note: The city of Campinas, SP is known for it's unique and artistic patterns of black and white stones on its sidewalks.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Cascavel Black Number Arrow
metas.note: A tiny black pole paint, containing a white number with a triangle-shaped arrow. Unique to Cascavel, Parana.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Cascavel Blue Lamp
metas.note: The town of Cascavel, Paraná uses this blue lamp. However, in newer coverage it is very rare to find.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Ceara Lamp Arms
metas.note: Lamps in Ceará often have a fancy and colourful arm, whether as lampposts or attached to utility poles. It sometimes says the town on the arm.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Ceara Poletop
metas.note: This assymetrical pole with no supports appears statewide in Ceara and sometimes Rondonia. (The Sao Paulo pole has a support bar)
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Center White Lines
metas.note: White Center lines are very common in Joao Pessoa. Yellow dashed lines are rare.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Chessboard Sidewalk
metas.note: The sidewalks with a chessboard pattern are common in Curitiba, PR.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/brazil for more clues.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Cobblestone Pavement
metas.note: Cobblestone pavement is most common in the northeast and in Rio Grande do Sul.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Colorful Signpost
metas.note: These colorful, thick signposts can be found in different cities in the state of Sao Paulo.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Compact Electricity Counter on Pole
metas.note:
An electricity counter with a compact design can be seen in Mato Grosso, Para, Amapa and Paraiba.

The "less compact" variant with several counters does not exist in Paraiba.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Concrete Trash Bins
metas.note: Brazil often uses metal trash baskets outside houses. In Acre and Rondônia, however, it is much more common to see them made of concrete.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Connector in Bend
metas.note: Meta for Sao Paulo. Only counts when the connector is pointing downwards. The connectors pointing upwards are generic.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Corroded Streetsign
metas.note: All the street signs in Palmas are corroded.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Crossbar with no support
metas.note: Crossbars with no support bars are almost exclusively found in Piaui, Ceara, Rio Grande do Norte and Alagoas. They also frequently appear in the North-East in general, and in Rondonia and Roraima.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Curitiba Sidewalk
metas.note: The two most typical sidewalk patterns in Curitiba, PR.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Dark Brown Insulator on Grey Base
metas.note: These dark brown insulators with grey bases are found almost exclusively in Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Divided Highway
metas.note: São Paulo has far more divided highways than any other state.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Embedded Pole ID
metas.note: Yellow plate embedded into pole. Mainly in Maranhao, spill into Para and Piaui.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Exremely Long Insulator
metas.note:
This one is basically a sub-category of the 6+ Ridge Insulator. It's common in Para, Parana, Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul.

However, it's not always easy to tell apart, but the longer the insulator feels, the more you should consider those states.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Insulators by samuel8170

metas.name: Infrastructure - Fancy Lamp - Campo Mourão
metas.note: "Fancy Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Campo Mourão.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Fancy Lamp - Cidade Gaucha
metas.note: "Fancy Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Cidade Gaucha. Notably, it's very similar to the one from Campo Mourao.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Fancy Lamp - Goioere
metas.note: "Fancy Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one - with the yellow support - is unique to the town of Goioere. However, in newer coverage, the yellow supports are rarer to find.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Fancy Lamp - Loanda
metas.note: "Fancy Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one - with a plain white lamp and no painted patterns on it - is unique to the town of Loanda.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Fancy Lamp - Umuarama
metas.note: "Fancy Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Umuarama. It is strikingly similar to the lamp from Cidade Gaucha.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Fancy Lamp - Umuarama
metas.note: "Fancy Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific, uniquely shaped one is unique to the town of Umuarama.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Florianopolis Pole
metas.note: Poles on Florianopolis, especially on Santa Catarina Island are painted white with blue and red stripes.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Florianopolis Sign
metas.note: Sometimes also with a white line instead of a red line.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Fortaleza ID
metas.note: These two types of IDs are common in Fortaleza (two pictures)
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Gamma + Box
metas.note:
Gamma pole with an electricity box at the end of the crossbeam. Most common in Belem, Salvador and Rio de Janeiro. Can appear occasionally in Ceara and Alagoas.

In RJ, they are particularly common in Sao Goncalo, but appear statewide.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Goias Pole ID
metas.note: The Goias pole ID uses yellow paint with black numbers or a black plate with yellow numbers. Unlike the Bahia and Pernambuco IDs, the ID consists exclusively of digits.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Grass Verge
metas.note: Grass verges between the sidewalk and the road are common in Curitiba.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Green Lamp
metas.note: There are three large cities with green lamps: Cuiaba, Manaus and Vitoria
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Hexagonal Pavement
metas.note: Roads with hexagonal concrete tiles can be found across Brazil, but they are more common in Santa Catarina and Minas Gerais.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - High attached ID
metas.note: Yellow plate attached by zip tie or metal strip. If it is higher up on the pole, it's in Pernambuco.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Holey Ladder Pole
metas.note: Ladder Poles with holes in them are very common in Joao Pessoa (but not unique)
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Horizontal Insulators
metas.note: Poles with horizontal insulators are very common in Pará and less so in Mato Grosso. They are rarely found in Acre, Amapá, Tocantins, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Horizontal Insulators with Top
metas.note: Poles that have one insulator on top and alternating horizontal insulators can be found in Mato Grosso and southern Acre. It is also very rare in Rio Grande do Sul.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Huge Electric Box on Pole
metas.note: Electric meter boxes can be seen in other cities, but in Cuiaba, there are usually 3-6 or even more on one pole.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Huge pole ID
metas.note: This rather large pole ID is common in Betim, Minas Gerais.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Imperatriz holey ID
metas.note: This city ID is distinct thanks to the holes on the sides.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Imperatriz Ornate Lamp
metas.note: Imperatriz, Maranhao
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Internet Poster
metas.note: Internet Advertisements attached to poles are very common in Natal. Mnemonic: Internatal :)
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Ipiranga Lamp
metas.note: These red lamps that resemble Belém lamps can be found in the neighborhood of Ipiranga in Florianopolis.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Irregular Cobblestone
metas.note: Cobblestone roads with randomly sized stones are most common in southeast Rio Grande do Sul and Minas Gerais.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Itumbiara Red Lamp
metas.note: Itumbiara, Goias
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Joao de Barro nests
metas.note: These spheres on top of utility poles are João-de-Barro nests. They are common across the south of Brazil.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Joao Pessoa Stone Pavement
metas.note: Distinct stone sidewalks & driveways in Joao Pessoa.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Joinville Lamp
metas.note: Joinville, Santa Catarina
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Joinville Street Sign
metas.note: Not to be confused with the Curitiba sign, which can also be attached to a pole.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Kilometer Marker with Phone Number
metas.note: Phone numbers can sometimes be seen underneath kilometre markers in São Paulo.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Lack of Poles
metas.note: Suspicious lack of poles, and curved lamp posts in their place, are indicative of Brasília.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Little Guy Lamp
metas.note: This cute lamp is unique to Gurupi.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Lollipop Insulators
metas.note: These insulators are spherical or cone shaped and suspended on a rod above the insulator bar. They are often referred to as “lollipop” insulators. They are very common in Rio Grande de Norte, Paraíba, Pernambuco, and more rarely, Sergipe.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Londrina Black Pole ID
metas.note: These black pole IDs are common in the state of Paraná, except for the capital Curitiba. If the black pole has a decimal marker (.) in the number, it's in Londrina.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Londrina Blue Number on Pole
metas.note: The town of Londrina, Paraná sometimes has little blue numbers painted on its poles.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Low Attached ID
metas.note: Yellow plate attached by zip tie or metal strip. If it is lower on the pole, it is RGDN.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - MA006
metas.note: Most of this road has a thick (1m) stripe of red dirt on the sides of the road. The road is oriented North-South and frequently shows Babassu palms
metas.footer: Source: Unique Roads of the World by Figsy

metas.name: Infrastructure - Macapa Lamp
metas.note: Macapa, Amapa
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Macapa Pole ID
metas.note: Macapa, Amapa
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Maceio Beach Lamp
metas.note: The large road next to the beach of Maceio has these unique lamp arms that go to one site and then cross the pole to the other side again. West of the Maceio port, they point to both sides of the road, while east of the Maceio port, they only point to one side.
metas.footer: Source: self-researched

metas.name: Infrastructure - Maceio ID
metas.note: These two IDs are rare but unique to Maceio.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Maceio Lamp
metas.note: Long posts with top arm bend and yellow or grey top dot at the bottom.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Maceio Streetsign
metas.note: Also available in blue.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Manaus Pole ID
metas.note: Pole IDs in Manaus are usually above the lamp attachment.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Maraba Skull Box
metas.note: Yellow skull stickers are common on electric boxes in Maraba.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - MGDS Flag
metas.note: In urban settings, state flags might show up. Might pay off sometimes.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/brazil for more clues.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Minas Gerais ID with 0/1
metas.note: These pole IDs are specific for Minas Gerais. If they start with 0 or 1, it's Belo Horizonte.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Natal ID
metas.note: Natal, Rio Grande do Norte
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Neon-Yellow Horizontal ID
metas.note: Neon-yellow horizontal IDs are specific to Sao Paulo. Do not confuse with Campo Grande or Vitoria (they have vertical, and smaller, neon-yellow IDs)
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Neon-Yellow Pole ID
metas.note: Neon-yellow, vertical IDs can be found in Campo Grande, MS and Vitoria, ES. Do not confuse with horizontal neon-yellow IDs (Sao Paulo)
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Onitel Sticker
metas.note: Unique to Luziania, GO
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Open Electric Box
metas.note: Open or trashed electric boxes appear frequently in Maraba and Santarém (both Para).
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Orange Lamp
metas.note: Orange Lamps are common in Belem.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Orange Lamp Arm
metas.note: Very common in Teresina, one of the most well-known urban Brazil metas.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Outer Dashed Lines
metas.note: Outer Dashed Lines can rarely be found in Rio Grande do Norte or other northeast states.
metas.footer: Source: self-researched by me and Figsy

metas.name: Infrastructure - Para specific Pole ID
metas.note: Pare uses these state-wide pole IDs.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Paraiba ID
metas.note: This ID is uncommon, but unique to Paraiba (most common in the capital Joao Pessoa).
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Paraiba Lamp
metas.note: The shape matters.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Parana Black Paint Pole ID
metas.note: Pole IDs in Paraná are usually made up of black paint and yellow or white painted text. They do not appear in the capital of Paraná: Curitiba.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess, Plonk It

metas.name: Infrastructure - Parana Black Square
metas.note: This tiny black paint is rarely found on larger poles in Paraná. Still worth a quick scan, especially in urban locs.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Parana Road Pole Paint
metas.note: Utility poles in Paraná on intersections are sometimes painted with the street name. This is because metal signs are expensive. This is also possible on Northern Rio Grande do Sul ladder poles. An exception is the town of Sinop, Mato Grosso.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess, PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - PARE on stone
metas.note: Stone road markings are unique to Caxias do Sul, RS.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Pencil Pole Top
metas.note: This little hat on the top, which makes the whole pole resemble a pencil, is most common in Rio de Janeiro, but can also be found in Manaus and Distrito Federal.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Piles of Dirt Meta
metas.note: Common in Boa Vista
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Pole Company
metas.note: Electricity company names in Brazil are commonly engraved onto the poles, with their names sometimes corresponding to state names. For example, CELPA stands for Para, COSERN for Rio Grande do Norte or COELCE for Ceara.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Pole Paint starting with letter
metas.note: Yellow paint with black numbers, starts with a letter. Possible in Bahia and Pernambuco. The letter is often specific to a town. Goias uses similar paint IDs, but they consist only of digits.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Pole-Attached Sign
metas.note: Some poles in Curitiba, PR have street signs attached to them. Curitiba still uses regular, generic street signs, though.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Pole-Wrapped Sign
metas.note: These blue pole-wrapped signs are unique to Campo Grande.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Porto Alegre ID
metas.note: Porto Alegre, Rio Grande do Sul
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Porto Velho Pole ID
metas.note: Porto Velho, Rondonia
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Recife Lamp
metas.note: Recife, Pernambuco
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Rectangle on Pole Arm
metas.note: Unique for Recife. Can be faded or even have different colors. It's the shape that matters.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Red Brick Pavement
metas.note: Some roads in Acre are made of red brick.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Red Gravel
metas.note: Most roads in Piauí have red gravel on the side of the road. Some roads in Generation 4 now have tarmac and kerbs, but some gravel shoulders remain.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Red Sticker on Lamp
metas.note: This red sticker below the lamp is unique to Fortaleza.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Rio Branco Special Lamp
metas.note: This lamp can be found on Av. Ceara in Rio Branco.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Rio de Janeiro Lamp
metas.note: Curvy lamp arm, usually big head.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Rio de Janeiro Landbridge
metas.note: This map west of the city of Rio de Janeiro is unique due to the water in the south, the roadlines (double yellow - double broken yellow - single broken white) and the little wall in the North. Rio mountains can be seen in most sections of the road to the North.
metas.footer: Source: Unique Roads of the World by Figsy

metas.name: Infrastructure - Rio De Janeiro Polepaint
metas.note: This yellow polepaint, similar to Sao Paulo, but with all numbers, can be found in Rio de Janeiro.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Rio de Janeiro Taxi
metas.note: Taxis in Rio de Janeiro are completely yellow.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Rio Weird Pole
metas.note: When there is something out of the ordinary happening with the pole, it's Rio de Janeiro.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Roraima Lamps
metas.note: Lamps in Roraima have a similar style but have different colours in the main cities. Boa Vista, Normandia, and Mucajaí have red lamps, Rorainópolis has blue lamps, Pacaraima and Iracema have green, and Caracaraí has yellow.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Round Pole
metas.note: Alongside ladder poles, round poles can often be found across the south of Brazil, especially São Paulo. These poles are cylindrical and made of concrete.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Salvador Lamp Arm ID
metas.note: Long yellow ID on the lamp arm, can be very hard to spot.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Salvador Sidewalk
metas.note: Unique sidewalk, can have other black and white broken tile patterns.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Santarem Lamp
metas.note: Santarem, Para
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Sao Luis ID
metas.note: This rare ID is specific to Sao Luis. However, the embedded Maranhao IDs are more common.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Sao Luis Pointy Lamp
metas.note: Pointy front of lamp head, blue or yellow top light.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Sao Paulo Lamp
metas.note: Straight long lamp neck, with tight top bend, usually thin head.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Sao Paulo Pole
metas.note:
Assymetrical crossbeam and insulator position with a long support bar reaching to the middle of the longer part of the crossbeam.

Extremely common in Sao Paulo, common in Rio Grande do Sul. Less common Rio de Janeiro, Espirito Santo and Mato Grosso do Sul (where it appears most oftenly in Tres Lagoas). Rare in Mato Grosso.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Sao Paulo Polepaint
metas.note: Sao Paulo Metropolitan Area has these yellow pole paints with a three letter code. The letters stand for the town. SPU is the most important code, standing for the main city.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Serra dos Orgaos
metas.note: This road can be found North of Rio de Janeiro (city). It is a concrete road with black tar behind the road lines.
metas.footer: Source: Unique Roads of the World by Figsy

metas.name: Infrastructure - Short Gamma + Box
metas.note: Short crossbeam, support bar and electricity box at the end of the crossbeam. Only found in Belem. (unlike the regular Gamma pole with box which can also be found in Salvador and Rio de Janeiro).
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Small Red Tactile Pavement
metas.note: Small tile, circular bumps, red tactile pavement is very common in Vitoria, ES. (Do not confuse with Florianopolis, which has large tile red tactile pavement).
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Southern Sidewalk
metas.note: You can often see pavements in Rio Grande do Sul that have brown tiles but are either jagged and random, or square. This style can sometimes be seen in Santa Catarina.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Speedbumps
metas.note: Yellow dashed lines and speedbumps are very common in Brasília. (but not unique)
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Spool Insulators
metas.note: These insulators have a shape resembling a spool of thread. They are found mostly in Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo, and have been seen in Ceará.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Square Paint ID
metas.note: This ID with two sections, the upper one being a square with a number in it, appears in Pernambuco.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Striped Curbs
metas.note: Black and white striped curbs are common in Boa Vista.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Surprising Wooden Pole
metas.note: In Porto Alegre, there is noticeably more foliage, cleaner, and more spacious than any other city which makes the common wooden poles look somewhat out of place.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Teresina ID
metas.note: Long & Horizontal ID
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Thick Bottom Insulator
metas.note:
They're found almost anywhere, but can still resolve some 50/50s:

They are only rarely found in Rio Grande do Norte.

Also they're less common in Pernambuco, Parana, Santa Catarina.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Insulators by samuel8170

metas.name: Infrastructure - Thin Long Insulator
metas.note: Insulators in Ceará can sometimes be uniquely long and thin. They are in Goiás too, but are rare.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Thin Red Stripe
metas.note: A road with a thin, red stripe out of gravel can be found east of Teresina, Piaui.
metas.footer: Source: Unique Roads of the World by Figsy

metas.name: Infrastructure - Tiny Lamp - Araruna
metas.note: "Tiny Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Araruna.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Tiny Lamp - Cianorte
metas.note: "Tiny Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Cianorte.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Tiny Lamp - Cruzeiro do Oeste
metas.note: "Tiny Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Cruzeiro do Oeste.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Tiny Lamp - Loanda
metas.note: "Tiny Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Loanda.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Tiny Lamp - Maringa
metas.note: "Tiny Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Maringa.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Tiny Lamp - Paranavai
metas.note: "Tiny Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Paranavai.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Tocantins specific lamp
metas.note: This lamp with a short arm and top light is specific to Tocantins.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Tocantins specific lamp
metas.note: This blue lamp with top light and the unique pattern on the underside is specific to Tocantins.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Tocantins specific lamp
metas.note: This long blue lamp with a top light and a unique pattern on the underside is specific to Tocantins.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Transparent Mushroom Insulator
metas.note: Transparent, mushroom-shaped insulators are common in Alagoas. They less frequently appear in Coastal Santa Catarina. Rarely, they also appear in coastal Rio Grande do Sul, coastal Sao Paulo and in Sergipe.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Insulators by samuel8170

metas.name: Infrastructure - Trident Pole
metas.note: Poles with these wide insulators in a trident formation are common in Maranhão. The insulator itself is common across many states, but not in this configuration.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Two Part Lamp - Goias Variant
metas.note:
2-part lamp, most commonly seen in Minas Gerais and Goias. This particular variant with a the pole visible underneath is more common in Goias.

Otherwise, this pole appears in Rio Grande do Norte and Rio Grande do Sul (very useful if you have North/South vibe), spill in Distrito Federal and extremely rarely in Para, Mato Grosso and Rondonia.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Two Part Lamp - Minas Gerais Variant
metas.note:
2-part lamp, most commonly seen in Minas Gerais and Goias. This particular variant - with both parts enveloping the lamp - is more common in Minas Gerais.

Otherwise, this pole appears in Rio Grande do Norte and Rio Grande do Sul (very useful if you have North/South vibe), spill in Distrito Federal and extremely rarely in Para, Mato Grosso and Rondonia.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Uberaba ID
metas.note: In Uberaba, pole IDs start with 2 or 3, and sometimes with 1. In Belo Horizonte, meanwhile, they start with 0 or 1. They do not appear in any other cities in MG.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Uneven Stone Pavement
metas.note: These uneven but mostly square stone roads are seen in western Rio Grande do Sul and west Santa Catarina. The soil will often be very dark in these regions too.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Vitoria Electric Boxes
metas.note: Metal electricity box, sandwiched between plastic electricity boxes are very common in Vitoria, ES.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Vitoria ID
metas.note: Red pole ID.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Vitoria Streetsign
metas.note: Unique streetsign design in Vitoria.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Weird Road Layout
metas.note: Roundabouts and weird layout roads that are mostly empty, and perfectly flat, are common in Palmas.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - White Mushroom Insulator
metas.note: Bahia uses these unique white insulators sometimes.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - WiFi-Password Pole-ID
metas.note: If you find pole IDs with codes that resemble WiFi-passwords (mix of digits, upper- and lowercase letters), you're in Curitiba, PR.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Wooden Pole
metas.note: Some states also use wooden poles. They are most commonly seen in Rio Grande do Sul, Roraima, Amazonas, and Rio de Janeiro.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure - Yellow Outer Lines
metas.note: Yellow outer lines on urban roads are very common in Curitiba.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Yellow Stick
metas.note: This yellow stick is common in Rio Branco, and often has a sign attached to it.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - Zig-Zag lamp arm
metas.note: In Brazil, this Zig-Zag lamp arm is unique to Caxias do Sul.
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Urban Metas by Cheddarman and Antidotess

metas.name: Infrastructure - ZigZag-Topbar
metas.note: This pole configuration, featuring a zigzag-shaped top bar resting atop a flat crossbar, is exclusive to Ceara and Roraima. The pole is usually much larger than a regular electricity pole.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Infrastructure -6+ Ridge Insulators
metas.note:
These insulators have six or more ridges.

Commonly found in:

  • Bahia, Tocantins, Maranhao
  • Para, Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul
  • Parana Santa Catarina

Uncommon in:

  • Acre, Rondonia, Amapa
  • Piaui, Goias, Sao Paulo, RGDS

Rarely in:

  • RGDN, Rio de Janeiro
metas.footer: Source: Brazil Insulators by samuel8170

metas.name: Landscape - Acre Landscape
metas.note: Acre has a unique landscape of small grass hills and sparsely growing trees. The roads often do not cut around the hills like in most of Brazil, but ride the hills instead. A similar landscape can also be seen near Maraba in the state of Pará.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Landscape - Amazon Rainforest
metas.note: The Amazon is a dense rainforest that compromises 40% of Brazil's total area. Not many roads are within it, but those that are, mostly go through either biodiverse forest or grassy hills with sparse trees.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Landscape - Amazonas 319
metas.note: The Amazonas 319 has a very lush, bright green and tropical landscape, as it cuts through the Amazon rainforest. The road is flat and mostly unpaved, featuring bright orange soil. However, closer to Manaus the road becomes paved. There are wooden or ladder poles alongside the entire stretch. It is covered by the blue Generation 4 car.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Landscape - BR-163 in Para
metas.note: The Pará section of the 163 is often hilly, curvy, dry, and sometimes hazy. It has a wide range of amazonian vegetation. The road is frequently trafficked, usually by transportation trucks. It is covered by the blue Generation 4 car.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Landscape - BR174 in Amazonas
metas.note: This road can be recognized by the Amazonian looking trees and the NW/SE angle. It always has Gen 4 and an exposed, blue car front.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/brazil for more clues.

metas.name: Landscape - BR230 in Amazonas
metas.note: This wide dirt road has Amazonian trees and a blurred car. You will not find other cars on the road. It's the only East-to-West angle road in that area.
metas.footer: Source: Unique Roads of the World by Figsy

metas.name: Landscape - BR230 in Para
metas.note: This road looks like an Amazonian road with the trees and dense rainforest. It runs east-west, slightly to the south. The road looks like its stained with mud
metas.footer: Source: Unique Roads of the World by Figsy

metas.name: Landscape - BR319, North of Porto Velho
metas.note: This road is characterized by it's Amazonian look and the SW-NE road angle. Some sections of this road are overcast and/or showcase a flat landscape.
metas.footer: Source: Unique Roads of the World by Figsy

metas.name: Landscape - Caatinga landscape
metas.note: Northeastern Brazil can be identified by its dry soil, shrubs and succulents (the Caatinga landscape).
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Landscape - Caatinga landscape - rain coverage
metas.note: Northeastern Brazil can be identified by its dry soil, shrubs and succulents (the Caatinga landscape). In rainy season coverage, the shrubs are still recognizable, but can be deceptively green.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Landscape - Corvo Branco
metas.note: This road in eastern Santa Catarina is characterized by its windyness and by the steep mountains and cliffs along its side. It can feel like your driving with the clouds. The road goes through Corvo Branco which is a famous tourist attraction.
metas.footer: Source: Unique Roads of the World by Figsy

metas.name: Landscape - Dunas da Sabiaguaba
metas.note: This road east of Fortaleza is characterized by its unique pavement and the sanddunes along the road.
metas.footer: Source: Unique Roads of the World by Figsy

metas.name: Landscape - Exposed Rock
metas.note: Espírito Santo, and the surrounding areas, often have large mountains with exposed rock.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Landscape - Flat Wetland
metas.note: Coastal regions in Rio Grande do Sul are recognisable due to being a rare flat wetland, which is uncommon in Brazil.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Landscape - Landbridge in Rio Grande do Sul
metas.note: Recognizable by the swamp-like landscape, the pine trees along the road and the Lagoon It runs at a SE-NW angle.
metas.footer: Source: Unique Roads of the World by Figsy

metas.name: Landscape - Noronha Rocks
metas.note: Ilha de Fernando de Noronha is similar in vegetation to NE-Brazil and has large exposed rocks.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Landscape - North of Uiramuta road
metas.note: This very unique looking road features rolling hills, which is unusual for the rather flat Roraima. It is a windy dirt road and despite being green, it lacks trees. What seperates this from the road south of Uiramuta is that it's more skinny and steeper.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/brazil for more clues.

metas.name: Landscape - Rio Grande do Sul Landscape
metas.note: The landscape in Rio Grande do Sul can be hilly or flat with lush, green fields. Southern areas can have some resemblance to Uruguay.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Landscape - Rollercoaster Road
metas.note: The 364 through Acre is very recognisable due to the rollercoaster-like landscape and road: the road uniquely rides the hills rather than snaking around them. There is usually no traffic, and is covered mostly by Generation 3 with an antenna.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Landscape - Roraima Landscape
metas.note: Rural locations in Roraima are mostly open grassy plains with large, distant mountains in the background. Occasionally, you are on roads within the mountains. Furthermore, the grass in Roraima is distinctly thin, and grows in bunches.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Landscape - Serra do Mar
metas.note:
Serra do Mar is a high mountain range that runs close to the coast from Parana to Northern RGDS.

If you have a high altitude road going on the mountains, instead of in the valleys, you're likely here.
metas.footer: Source: self-researched

metas.name: Landscape - South of Uiramuta
metas.note: This very unique looking road features rolling hills, which is unusual for the rather flat Roraima. It is a windy dirt road and despite being green, it lacks trees. What seperates this from the road south of Uiramuta is that it's less skinny and less steep.
metas.footer: Source: Unique Roads of the World by Figsy

metas.name: Landscape - Southeast Hills
metas.note: Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo often have rolling grassy hills.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Landscape - Swampy Road
metas.note: A very swampy road (PA-154) can be found Northwest of Belém. Notably, there are very few trees, and the soil is very red.
metas.footer: Source: Unique Roads of the World by Figsy

metas.name: Landscape - Uneven Stone + Corn
metas.note: This beautiful road west of Cascavel and South of Toledo, by the PR-585 is characterized by the uneven red stone pavement and the corn plantation next to it.
metas.footer: Source: Unique Roads of the World by Figsy

metas.name: Trekker - Amazonian Trekker
metas.note: This Amazonian trekker combines boat and walking coverage on and near the Madeira and Aripuana rivers, south of the 319. They are seen travelling through dense rainforest and small villages.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Trekker - Lençóis Maranhenses National Park
metas.note: The beautiful National Park of Northeast Maranhão, known for its sand dunes with pools of water, has walking trekker and vehicle coverage. The truck is white with a black bed. The landscape can vary from beach to sandy wetland.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Trekker - Noronha Boat Trekker
metas.note: There is boat coverage around the island of Ilha de Fernando de Noronha.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Vegetation - Acai Palm
metas.note:
Açai palms produce fruits that are popular globally. Most of these palms are found near Belem, but can be seen across the Amazon. They are distinct in the way the leaflets droop downward along with their unusually thin trunks.

Note by MB: They are very similar to the Jucara Palm (which grows in Southern Brazil). Tips for differentiation:

  • Acai Palms have more thick, robust leaves (comparatively)
  • Acai Palms like growing in bunches
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Vegetation - Acrocomia Totai (Paraguay Palm)
metas.note:
This palm is commonly mistaken to be a Macaw Palm (Acrocomia Aculeata). The key difference is that the trunk of the "Paraguay Palm" is often smoother and less irregular. The crown can also give some hints although it's difficult to catch the differences

  • Macaw Palm: More open and irregular, with leaves spreading in different directions.
  • "Paraguay Palm": Denser and more compact, sometimes looking neater and rounder.

The distribution is also a bit different, as this palm usually is closer to Paraguay than the Macaw Palm which stretches further.
metas.footer: Source: A Learnable Plant World - Palms by Zen

metas.name: Vegetation - Babassu Palm
metas.note: Babassu palms have long, robust leaves comprised of many leaflets. Trunk length can vary from short to tall. They are found throughout the Amazon, or more rarely, down the east coast.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Vegetation - Carnauba Palm
metas.note: Carnaúba palms have short but strong, fan-like leaves and a trunk that is smooth at the top and spiked at the bottom. They are common in Ceará but are also in Piauí and Rio Grande do Norte.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Vegetation - Coconut Palm
metas.note: Coconut palm trees have long leaves, can grow very tall, and have thin trunks. They are common across the north eastern states and sometimes further west or south along the coast.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Vegetation - Jucara Palm
metas.note:
Closely related to the Açaí palm, they are really hard to distinguish apart from each other. However, the Açaí palm grows mostly in the northern flat regions of Brazil, while the Juçara grows in the mountainous south-east regions of Brazil anywhere from Espirito Santo down to Rio Grande do Sul.

Here some tips for differences:

  • The leaves of Jucara Palms are thinner
  • Jucara Palms have more space, they don't like growing close to each other.
metas.footer: Source: A Learnable Plant World - Palms by Zen

metas.name: Vegetation - Macaw Palm
metas.note: Macaw palms, often called Paraguay palms, have thin leaves compared to other palms, and often have a visible spear shaped top. They are very common around Mato Grosso do Sul and the surrounding states, but can be seen much further out sometimes. These palms should be used with caution, and single trees are much less of an indicator than multiple trees.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Vegetation - Moriche Palm
metas.note: Moriche palms have leaves with a rounded fan shape. They are most common in Amazonas, Acre, and Roraima, but can be found in all of the Amazonian states.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Vegetation - Mysterious Northeastern Plant
metas.note: This species of plant, with long stems and many leaves growing up, are very common in Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, and Paraíba. In the dry season, you can still make out the distinct long stems without leaves.

metas.name: Vegetation - Parana Pine
metas.note: These distinct trees, called Paraná pines, have long horizontal branches with leaves only at the end. They grow mainly in the southern Brazilian states of Paraná, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Vegetation - Pine Trees
metas.note: Pine Trees are common in Southern Brazil, but are rarely ever found north of Belo Horizonte.
metas.footer: Source: self-researched

metas.name: Vegetation - Queen Palm
metas.note:
Queen palms have leaf stems that point upwards on the trunk and then "bow down" again to the ground due to gravity. They are native to South America. In Brazil, they are mainly found along the coast between Rio de Janeiro and Porto Alegre.

Outside of South America, they're also found in Florida and East Coast Queensland.
metas.footer: Source: self-researched

metas.name: Vegetation - Tocantins Grass
metas.note: Very tall grass can be often seen in the centre of the country, most notably in the Tocantins, Goiás, Bahia, and Minas Gerais states.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt
